projects.title: SaveSip / Cup$i
projects.summary: A gamified drink-spending tracker that turns small café purchases into visible savings habits.

caseStudy.problem: Small coffee, boba, and café purchases feel harmless in the moment, but repeated purchases add up. Traditional budgeting tools can feel cold or spreadsheet-heavy.
caseStudy.direction: Cup$i evolved into SaveSip: a warmer product story using mascots, challenges, savings feedback, and a community/recipe layer.
caseStudy.audience: Audience statements and a persona were developed during research (see the persona artifact below).
caseStudy.research: Research before polish: audience statements, notes, personas, low-fidelity flows, and high-fidelity interface planning.
features: Sip mood, levels, unlockables, and challenges
caseStudy.visual: Friendly mascots — Sip (“Saving feels good!”) and Spendy (“Overspending hurts!”) — make financial feedback emotionally approachable. The Cup$i logo system carried the original identity.
caseStudy.goal: Make saving feel visual, fast, rewarding, and emotionally approachable.
caseStudy.status: Concept case study (academic / independent practice). No launch metrics are claimed.

projects.title: SmartCart
projects.summary: Discovery sprint for faster grocery-list creation, repeat buys, useful customization, and user-controlled smart suggestions.
projects.source: Master Portfolio p. 9 (SmartCart Research Packet, Sprint 1, Feb 21 2026); Creative Resume

caseStudy.problem: Current shopping list apps often feel tap-heavy, overly simplified, and limited to cosmetic customization (themes) rather than functional customization (quantity, units, notes). Some apps ask users to input unreliable information such as item prices, which slows list creation and varies by store, taxes, and promotions.
caseStudy.audience: Defining the target audience was itself a research goal: “Use evidence to define target audience, core problem, and MVP scope.”
researchMeta: SmartCart (shopping list app with repeat-buy suggestions + item customization)
Competitive audits (direct + indirect), secondary research (reviews + literature)
goals: Understand how people currently plan grocery trips and create lists.
Identify the top friction points in list creation and in-store use.
Learn how people handle repeat buys / staples and how they decide restock timing.
Define trust boundaries for smart suggestions vs auto-add behavior.
Use evidence to define target audience, core problem, and MVP scope.
questions: What triggers a grocery trip and how do people plan it?
How do people keep track of staples and repeat items?
What makes list creation feel slow or annoying?
What item-level details do users actually want to save (quantity, units, notes, store)?
What makes smart suggestions feel helpful vs intrusive?
hypotheses: People do not mind making lists; they mind rewriting the same staples repeatedly.
Too many taps (or high effort) causes users to fall back to Notes/Reminders.
Functional customization matters more than theme customization.
Smart suggestions are welcomed when they are transparent and user-controlled.
focus: Functional customization: quantity, units, notes, store
Trust boundaries for suggestions vs. auto-add
Affinity mapping, HMW questions, and MVP prioritization
caseStudy.principle: Smart suggestions should be transparent, useful, and controlled by the user.
caseStudy.next: The documented work covers the discovery sprint: planning, research questions, and hypotheses. Interview findings, wireframes, and high-fidelity screens are not part of the source material yet, so they are shown here as next steps rather than completed work.
caseStudy.status: Research-stage product concept. Hypotheses are untested; no results or metrics are claimed.

images.alt: First page of the SmartCart Research Packet: project table, research overview, research goals, key research questions, and hypotheses to test.
images.caption: SmartCart Research Packet — Discovery / Research Sprint 1

projects.title: Crosswalks That Explain Themselves
projects.summary: A smart-city proposition focused on trust, clarity, accessibility, and fast public decisions.

caseStudy.problem: The project focuses on Smart City pedestrian crossings as an IoT interaction problem. The core issue is whether users can understand and trust smart systems in fast public moments.
caseStudy.audience: Pedestrians at public crossings — a public-facing context where decisions are fast and accessibility needs vary.
caseStudy.research: The project explores how small, clear interface cues can make crossings feel safer and more legible.
caseStudy.proposal: nowWhat — a public-facing pedestrian crossing interface with small, context-aware intent cues. The cue appears only when normal crossing logic changes or extra clarity is needed. The system supports confidence without clutter or requiring a phone app.
states: The crossing is approached; the display stays quiet unless clarity is needed.
The pedestrian is waiting for the crossing to change.
Normal crossing logic has changed or the system is uncertain; the interface explains instead of failing silently.
caseStudy.status: Concept proposal. Interface states are defined; no deployment or test results are claimed.

projects.title: Berry Vibes Digital Cookbook
projects.summary: A continuous recipe website combining original recipe sketches, branding, typography, information design, and animated scrolling.
body: A continuous digital cookbook built from personal recipes, playful branding, custom recipe sketches, and animated web interactions.

From placeholders to original recipe sketches: stock food images were temporary during development; the final visual direction replaced them with custom hand-drawn recipe artwork so the website feels authored, cohesive, and connected to the Berry Vibes identity.
Project story: Concept → Mockups → Prototype → Custom illustration → Final website.
